1.pericope_label: The six sons born to David in Hebron, and the four born of Bathsheba in Jerusalem

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch rule out the easy answer to the name discrepancy on principle: the difference between Daniel here and Chileab in Samuel cannot well have arisen through an error of a copyist, and is probably to be explained on the supposition that this son had two different names. They note that the six sons born in Hebron are enumerated also in Samuel with mention of their mothers as here, and explain the singular verb after a plural subject as a point of syntax; of the Jerusalem sons they count thirteen, four of them Bathsheba’s, and observe that the thirteen names are enumerated again later in this book and in the parallel in Samuel. Ellicott keeps closely to the wording throughout, preferring a second, Daniel, to Abigail, and noting that Samuel adds of her what this list omits, that she had been the wife of Nabal. He observes that the common Hebrew text reads to Absalom where a number of manuscripts and all the old versions read simply Absalom, and reports Kimchi’s characteristic explanation that the longer form alludes to a phrase meaning not Absalom, that is, no father of peace but a rebel. Of Eglah he holds that she is not marked out as a principal wife and that the words his wife are added simply to balance the clause, making up for the absence of those details of her connexions which are supplied for the other wives, and he calls the Jewish identification of her with Michal groundless. He adds that the notice of the length of David’s reign first in Hebron and then in Jerusalem is not read in the parallel section of Samuel, though the same statements occur elsewhere there.

Clarke supplies two rabbinic explanations of the double name, and they are not of a piece: the Targum has the son called Chileab because he was in every respect like to his father, the word itself importing like to the father; but Jarchi accounts for it from a doubt about his paternity, since David took Abigail immediately after Nabal’s death and it could not be ascertained whether the child were David’s son or Nabal’s, so that he was named Daniel, God is my judge, as well as Chileab. On Eglah he reports that the Targum and Jarchi and others maintain she was Michal, Saul’s daughter, objects that this does not well agree with the statement that Michal had no child to the day of her death, and then leaves the door ajar by allowing that she might have had a child before that time. Of Bathsheba’s two names he makes it a copyist’s slip outright, one Hebrew letter having been put by mistake for another; and he notes that Solomon is named last of the four although he was the eldest of them, because the genealogy was to be continued from him. Wesley takes the phrase his wife in the opposite sense from Ellicott, as marking Eglah out: possibly she is so called because she was his first and therefore most proper wife, her son standing sixth only because he was born after the rest.

Gill says briefly that the second son had two names, and reports without comment that the Targum makes Eglah to be Michal, Saul’s daughter. Of the Jerusalem sons he counts nine where the parallel gives seven, and observes that Bathsheba is here called Bathshua and her father Ammiel where elsewhere he is Eliam, treating these as names of much the same signification rather than as errors.

Henry reads the list for its griefs rather than its names. David had many sons, and happy is the man that has his quiver full of such arrows; but some of them were a grief to him, Amnon and Absalom and Adonijah, and we do not read of any that imitated his piety or devotion except Solomon, who came far short of it. One of them, borne to him by Bathsheba, he called Nathan, probably in honour of Nathan the prophet, who had reproved him for his sin in that very matter and been instrumental in bringing him to repentance; it seems he loved the prophet the better for it as long as he lived, from which Henry draws that it is wisdom to esteem those our best friends who deal faithfully with us. He adds that it was from this son of David that our Lord descended as man.

8.pericope_label: The rest of David’s sons and Tamar their sister, and the kings of Judah from Solomon to Josiah

schools.summary: Clarke lays out the arithmetic of the disagreement with Samuel: there are thirteen if the four sons of Bathsheba are counted and nine without them, while Samuel gives eleven with those four and only seven without. He resolves it by supposing that Samuel reckoned only those then living where the chronicler takes in the dead as well, and adds Jarchi’s alternative, that the duplicated names are what raise the regular seven to nine and that the dead who left no posterity are named to swell the number of David’s descendants. Of Tamar he notes that she is the only daughter of David whose name is on record, although he is said elsewhere to have had both sons and daughters. Wesley reaches the same solution as Clarke more briefly, that two are omitted in Samuel because they died very early, whereas here we have all the sons of David.

Ellicott draws a different conclusion from the comparison with Samuel, that the differences make it improbable these lists were drawn from that source at all. He alone explains why one name has shifted its form: the form meaning the Lord knoweth, which stands later in this book, he judges the more ancient, though Samuel too has the form meaning God knoweth; for God was of old called Baal as well as El, and the former title was discarded only because it tended to foster a confusion between the degrading cultus of the Canaanite Baals and the true religion of Israel, so that in later times men grew unwilling to write or speak the name at all and in compound names substituted either El or Iah, as here, or else the word for shame, which is how Ishbosheth came to stand where an older form had Baal in it. Of the concubines he observes that they are mentioned several times in Samuel but their sons only here, and grants the difficulty plainly, that however repugnant to modern ideas it was and is part of the state of an Oriental potentate to possess a harem of many wives; of Tamar he says she was not the only sister but the one whose unhappy fate had made her famous. Through the line of kings he works as a philologist, giving the sense of name after name, so that the succession shows itself almost wholly composed of names compounded with the divine name, with Manasseh standing out as perhaps of Egyptian origin. Keil and Delitzsch carry the succession through to the sons of Josiah and then to the descendants of the captive and exiled Jeconiah.

Henry reads the line of kings for what it leaves out. David having nineteen sons, we may suppose them to have raised many noble families in Israel of whom we never hear in the history; but scripture gives an account only of the descendants of Solomon here and of Nathan in the gospel. The rest had the honour to be the sons of David, while these alone had the honour of being related to the Messiah — the sons of Nathan being his fathers as man, and the sons of Solomon his predecessors as king.

Gill marks the divisions of the list rather than its difficulties, noting that these were the sons by David’s wives with the concubines’ sons following, and that from the tenth verse to the end of the fourteenth the successors of David are reckoned in the order of their reign, down to Josiah and his sons.

17.pericope_label: The sons of Jeconiah in captivity, the line of Zerubbabel, and the generations to Elioenai

schools.summary: Clarke asks who Assir was and answers possibly nobody, since the Hebrew word signifies a prisoner and may be taken as an epithet of Jeconiah, who was a very long time a prisoner in Babylon; Salathiel, he notes, was the son of Jeconiah, as the gospel genealogy has it. On the prophecy that Jeconiah should be childless he answers that it must refer to his posterity being deprived of the throne, and that the prophet interprets himself in saying that no man of his seed shall prosper on the throne of David. For the difficulty about Zerubbabel’s father he reports a bold solution, that the words should simply be omitted, Pedaiah being wanting in the Syriac and Arabic, which would leave Zerubbabel the son of Salathiel as the gospel has him; and he passes on a conjecture that the verse should rather read that the sons of Salathiel were Malchiram and Pedaiah. Where the text numbers six and names five he finds the versions no help and the manuscripts no correction, and concludes that either the father is counted with his sons or a name has been lost out of the text. Wesley glosses the same disputed word as of Jeconiah the captive, added to show that he begot his son while a prisoner in Babylon; takes the sentence about Pedaiah to be short and imperfect, as is frequent in Hebrew, with something understood; and on the number six allows that the father may be included, but then suggests what none of the others consider, that the Hebrew word rendered six may itself be the proper name of one of the sons.

Ellicott reaches the same reading of the disputed word by two arguments of his own: it accords with the Masoretic punctuation, which joins the term to Jeconiah, and it accounts for the offspring of Jeconiah being mentioned twice over, so that Zedekiah is separated from the sons born in captivity; he would render the clause, the sons of Jeconiah when captive, Shealtiel his son. He keeps the Hebrew of the following verse as it stands, by which six persons arranged as two trios are sons of Jeconiah and brothers of Shealtiel, and he finds the exile written into their names, one being a compound Babylonian name whose parts seem to mean that the moon-god should protect — such a name as might well be given to a Jewish prince at the court of Babylon, just as Daniel and his three companions received idolatrous designations of the same sort. Of Zerubbabel he notes that the name means born at Babel while his father is appropriately named, meaning Iah hath redeemed, and that he is called son of Shealtiel in the prophets and in Ezra and in the gospel. On the shortfall of names he looks to the versions, which at the preceding verse represent an important variant, the Greek turning what the Hebrew gives as several parallel families into a single descending line of son after son. He also makes the list yield dates, identifying one of the last names with the Hattush whom Ezra records going up with him in the second return and reckoning him of the fourth generation after Zerubbabel, and placing the sons at the very end of the chapter in the sixth generation from Zerubbabel, living under Artaxerxes Ochus — though if the Greek reading of the earlier verse is right their date falls four generations later. Keil and Delitzsch carry the lists through without comment to the descendants of the captive Jeconiah and the families that follow.

Gill answers the prophecy of childlessness as Clarke does, that it respects not his having no children in any sense but his having none to succeed him in the kingdom. On Zerubbabel’s father he declines the easiest way out, the suggestion of Grotius and others that this is a different Zerubbabel, for which he sees no reason, and offers instead either that Pedaiah was himself a son of Salathiel so that Zerubbabel as grandson may be called his son, as Kimchi thinks, or rather that Salathiel, having no children, adopted his brother’s son and made him his successor in the government.
